content: Fibromyalgia is a condition characterized by chronic, widespread pain that significantly reduces physical function. Exercise is often recommended as a treatment to manage its symptoms. Resistance training, a form of exercise involving progressive resistance to improve muscle strength, endurance, and power, has been studied for its potential benefits in individuals with fibromyalgia. The objective of this research was to evaluate the benefits and potential harms of resistance training in adults with fibromyalgia. The study compared resistance training to control groups and other forms of exercise, such as aerobic or flexibility training. A comprehensive search of nine electronic databases and other sources was conducted, with the last search performed on March 5, 2013. Out of 1,865 citations, five studies met the inclusion criteria. These criteria required the studies to be randomized clinical trials, include adults diagnosed with fibromyalgia based on established criteria, and provide data comparing resistance training to other interventions. A total of 219 women with fibromyalgia participated in these studies, with 95 assigned to resistance training programs. The included studies varied in their design. Three trials compared 16 to 21 weeks of moderateto high-intensity resistance training to a control group. Two studies compared eight weeks of progressive resistance training (using free weights or body weight) to aerobic training, such as treadmill walking. One study compared 12 weeks of low-intensity resistance training (using light hand weights and elastic tubing) to flexibility exercises involving static stretches. The results showed statistically significant improvements in several outcomes for participants in resistance training programs compared to control groups. These included: Multidimensional function, as measured by the Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire (FIQ), with a reduction of 16.75 points on a 100-point scale (95% CI: -23.31 to -10.19). Self-reported physical function, with a reduction of 6.29 points on a 100-point scale (95% CI: -10.45 to -2.13). Pain, with a reduction of 3.3 cm on a 10-cm scale (95% CI: -6.35 to -0.26). Tenderness, with a reduction of 1.84 tender points out of 18 (95% CI: -2.6 to -1.08). Muscle strength, with an increase of 27.32 kg force on bilateral concentric leg extension (95% CI: 18.28 to 36.36). When comparing resistance training to aerobic training, no statistically significant differences were found in multidimensional function, self-reported physical function, or tenderness. However, aerobic training showed a statistically significant reduction in pain (0.99 cm on a 10-cm scale; 95% CI: 0.31 to 1.67) compared to resistance training. In comparisons between resistance training and flexibility exercises, resistance training demonstrated statistically significant improvements in multidimensional function (6.49 FIQ units on a 100-point scale; 95% CI: -12.57 to -0.41) and pain (0.88 cm on a 10-cm scale; 95% CI: -1.57 to -0.19). However, no significant differences were observed for tenderness or muscle strength. The quality of evidence was rated as low due to the small number of studies and methodological concerns, such as poor reporting of allocation concealment, lack of blinding of outcome assessors, and absence of pre-specified protocols. Adverse effects were poorly documented, but no serious adverse events were reported. Attrition rates did not differ significantly between intervention groups. In conclusion, low-quality evidence suggests that moderateto high-intensity resistance training can improve multidimensional function, pain, tenderness, and muscle strength in women with fibromyalgia. Additionally, eight weeks of aerobic exercise may be more effective than moderate-intensity resistance training for pain reduction. Low-intensity resistance training over 12 weeks may also be superior to flexibility exercises for improving pain and multidimensional function. Importantly, women with fibromyalgia appear to be able to safely engage in moderateto high-intensity resistance training.
